name: Beckey-Davis

pitch_detail.notes: Climb the left-side chimney between two prominent V-shaped features on the south face; move left atop the chimney onto knobby terrain to belay.
Sustained knobby face, slabs, and cracks up toward a gully/chimney system; route-finding is somewhat ambiguous through this stretch on the way to Snafflehound Ledge.
Traverse right across the obvious Snafflehound Ledge to a small tree, then a short steep step to the base of the crux pitch.
Route crux: a shallow left-facing dihedral forces you right until an overhang forces a step-across left into a flaring jam crack; eases above the bulge on face holds and chicken-heads.
Crack system/steep gully bypassing a chockstone on the left to the small notch east of the summit horn; watch for loose blocks in the gully.

Delicate friction traverse on a ramp finishing on a good jam crack to the summit; a harder 5.10a thin-hands splitter variant climbs straight out of the notch for parties wanting more technical finish.

rappel_detail.pull: This is the station where ropes hang up. One party's rope jammed on the pull off the first rappel and had to be freed by hauling on it with a progress-capture pulley. Pull from as far out from the chute as the ledge allows.
rappel_detail.notes: Noticeably shorter than the four rappels below it; the rest of the line runs close to a full 30 m.
rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed webbing at the true summit, no bolts. What is actually there has changed: a 2018 party found a home-made spinning hanger backed up to a rock pinch, and the local rangers stripped and rebuilt the tat on the lower (west) summit stations that same season because the accumulated slings had become impossible to judge.
hazards: The start is awkward — you squeeze into a narrow chute to get weight onto the rope, which is the least pleasant transition on the descent
Abandoned stations sit further climber's left of the current line and are explicitly not recommended; do not follow old tat leftward
rappel_detail.station: Essentially underfoot once you top out — the flat ground at the true summit. Parties who finish the West Ridge on the lower west summit should not expect an anchor there; at least one party in 2018 found nothing on the west summit and had to continue east to the true summit to start the descent.

rappel_detail.notes: Every station on this line is tat, not fixed hardware; carry cord and be willing to replace rather than add to it.
rappel_detail.anchor: Webbing around a chockstone jammed between the main wall and a protruding flake. Relocated by the climbing rangers in 2018 — it is no longer on the big ledge where it used to be.
hazards: Cramped stance — the relocated station is on a pillar-like perch that is hard to stand at comfortably with two people
Missing it means either climbing back up or committing to unknown ground below
rappel_detail.station: Not visible from the summit. Rappel roughly 25 m and look climber's left. Relative to the old ledge station it sits about 30 ft (9 m) climber's left and about 50 ft (15 m) further down the slope, so parties navigating from a pre-2018 description will rappel straight past where they expect it.

rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed webbing (tat). No bolts anywhere on this descent.
rappel_detail.station: The one easy station on the line — from station 2 it is in plain sight directly below you.

rappel_detail.pull: Reported as having a great many places for the rope to jam. Flick the strands clear of the alcove and the gully edges before the last climber pulls, and think about which side you pull from.
rappel_detail.notes: After this rappel you can leave the ropes packed and downclimb 3rd class ground climber's right to reach the climbers' trail back to the base of the West Ridge — that scrambling is loose. Optionally, one or two more rappels from stations climber’s right of the gully drop straight onto the climbers’ path instead, rejoining the older rappel line: cleaner ground for more rope work.
hazards: The station sits directly beneath a large volume of loose rock, and getting down from it without knocking anything off is genuinely difficult — keep the rest of the party out from underneath and expect to be hit by what you dislodge yourself
The gully below is broken and full of snag features
Skipping the optional lower stations in favour of the downclimb puts you on loose 3rd class ground with a pack and a rope on your back.

If you take the optional lower stations, the last rappel is where stuck ropes are most often reported on this face, in one case with the far strand jamming about 10 m from its end and costing a party the rest of their daylight. Keep the strands separated and pull from ground clear of the flakes above.
rappel_detail.station: Hidden, and the station people miss. From station 3 you must trend climber's left rather than straight down; it is tucked into a small alcove left of station 3, sitting just above the gully where the ground eases off to 3rd and 4th class.

rappels: 4 single-rope rappels down the north face from the summit bolt on a 60 m rope, then a 3rd-class downclimb to the climbers’ path; one or two optional extra rappels replace the downclimb.
descent_text: From the summit, descend the north face on four single-rope rappels using a single 60m rope, then downclimb 3rd-class ground to the climbers’ path; two optional rappels from stations climber’s right of the gully can replace that downclimb. The first rap station is an old bolt at the true summit (reported to predate the 1980s); the second rappel is built around a wedged block that looks sketchy but has held for decades of parties. Remaining stations are slung natural anchors (webbing/tat) — carry extra material to back up aged slings. From the climbers’ path, scramble around to the base of the West Ridge; some parties report one more short rappel from that notch to regain the south-face base. Total time from summit back to packs is roughly 2 hours in a typical trip report.
approach: Standard access is via Aasgard Pass into the Core Enchantments: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Stuart Lake Trail (2.5 mi) → Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, crossing Mountaineer Creek and switchbacking up to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.1 mi/2,000 ft). From the south-end boulder field, climb Aasgard Pass (1.25 mi, ~2,000 ft of steep, loose scree/dirt — the crux of the approach, hazardous under lingering snow into early July with a hidden creek/moat beneath the talus, and avalanche-prone in shoulder season). From the 7,841-ft pass, travel cross-country through the Core past Tranquil and Isolation lakes toward Gnome Tarn and the base of Prusik's south face, roughly 7.5–8 miles and 4,600+ ft one-way. Note that this trailhead/pass can close seasonally (e.g., wildfire closures have forced parties onto the Snow Lakes Trail instead, which one trip report clocked at about 10 miles and 6,000+ ft, roughly 5 hours 44 minutes car-to-base — notably longer and with a different, less direct final approach past Lake Viviane to a climbers' trail on Prusik's south ridge).
overview: The original line up Prusik's south face (FA Fred Beckey and Dan Davis, June 1962). The lower pitches are comparatively unremarkable knobby face and slab climbing, but the upper half above Snafflehound Ledge delivers sustained, steep 5.9 crack climbing to the summit.
beta: Seven pitches from 5.5 to 5.9, starting up a chimney left of two prominent V-shaped features on the south face, crossing a long chimney-gully to Snafflehound Ledge, then finishing with a forced rightward dihedral/jam-crack crux and a choice of two summit finishes.
gear: Cams to 4 inches, with doubles in the 0.5–2 range for the sustained crack pitches
Full set of nuts/chocks — several belays rely on gear placements, not bolts
A couple of extra larger cams if you have them, useful on the crux pitch
Helmet — loose rock reported on the lower pitches
Long alpine slings to cut drag on the wandering, traversing pitches
